lesson.title: The Secret Meeting That Rewrote the Rules
lesson.summary: Meeting in Philadelphia from May to September 1787, the Constitutional Convention was called to fix the Articles of Confederation but instead produced an entirely new framework of government, the United States Constitution.
lesson.body:
By the spring of 1787, the failures of the Articles of Confederation were impossible to ignore. Shays' Rebellion had shown the national government could not keep order, and years of unpaid debts and interstate trade disputes had shown it could barely function day to day. Delegates from twelve states, every state except Rhode Island, gathered in Philadelphia beginning in May 1787 with instructions to revise the Articles of Confederation.

They met at the Pennsylvania State House, the same building where the Declaration of Independence had been debated and signed eleven years earlier, and which history would later call Independence Hall. George Washington, whose presence lent the gathering enormous credibility, was elected to preside over the proceedings. James Madison of Virginia arrived having studied ancient and modern confederacies in detail, and his careful daily notes remain the best record of what was said inside the closed doors, since the delegates agreed to keep their debates secret and even nailed the windows shut against eavesdroppers despite the summer heat.

It quickly became clear that revision would not be enough. Madison and the Virginia delegation arrived with a bold proposal, soon called the Virginia Plan, calling for an entirely new government with a strong national executive, a national judiciary, and a legislature with representation based on state population. Smaller states balked, fearing domination by Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Massachusetts, and William Paterson of New Jersey countered with the New Jersey Plan, which kept the existing structure of equal state representation but gave Congress somewhat more power, including limited taxation and trade authority.

The convention spent much of the summer working through the resulting deadlock, along with equally difficult disputes over how enslaved people should count toward representation and taxation, and how much power the new national government should hold over the states. These arguments would be resolved through what became known as the Great Compromise and the Three-Fifths Compromise, hammered out over weeks of tense negotiation among delegates who often disagreed sharply but shared a conviction that the existing system could not survive much longer.

Fifty-five delegates in total took part over the course of the summer, including Benjamin Franklin, then eighty-one years old and the convention's most senior statesman, and Alexander Hamilton, who represented New York but was frequently outvoted by his own state's other delegates. Rhode Island's absence was no accident either; its leaders were suspicious of any plan to strengthen the central government and simply declined to send anyone at all.

On September 17, 1787, thirty-nine of the remaining delegates signed the finished Constitution, while a handful of others, including George Mason and Edmund Randolph of Virginia, refused to add their names because they felt the document still lacked adequate protections for individual liberty. Sending the Constitution to the states for ratification set off a fierce national debate over whether this new, far stronger government should be adopted at all, a debate that would need nine of thirteen state conventions to say yes before the new government could even begin.
